title: What would close the loop between seeing and doing?
dek: The next questions sit between fields: maintaining scene state, testing physical hypotheses, creating useful training worlds, and measuring the effect on real decisions.
intro: Across the preceding chapters, the same problem reappears in different forms: a representation can be useful for one objective while leaving another underdetermined. Object labels omit contact geometry; rendered appearance does not identify mass or friction; a generated room need not be navigable; a sensible plan can fail during execution. These are interfaces at which research claims need to be tested.

The directions below are questions that emerge when those pieces are placed together. They are proposals for experiments and systems, not claims that one existing method has already solved the whole loop.

sections.heading: Persistent scene state after interaction
paragraphs: An open-vocabulary map can help an agent find the cabinet, but opening the door changes both visible geometry and accessibility. A persistent representation must preserve identity while revising pose, joint state, visibility, and relations. ConceptGraphs and VLMaps illustrate the value of queryable spatial memory; articulated tracking work such as CAPTRA highlights a different requirement, maintaining part state across observations. Combining these capabilities requires an explicit treatment of change. [cite:conceptgraphs] [cite:vlmaps] [cite:captra]

A revealing test would revisit a room before and after controlled object motions. It should separate a genuinely new object from a familiar one in a new state, count stale-map errors, and check whether map corrections improve later actions. Simply retaining every frame can hide the problem by storing mutually inconsistent evidence.

This also motivates selective memory. A mobile robot cannot retain every dense observation indefinitely at full resolution. A research question is which details to retain for future goals, which to compress, and when a compressed scene model should trigger another observation.

sections.heading: Turn uncertain geometry into a question the robot can test
paragraphs: A closed cabinet can conceal its interior and leave multiple joint hypotheses compatible with the visible surface. Interaction can supply information unavailable from passive observation. Ditto uses observations across interaction to build an articulated digital twin; UMPNet and Where2Explore connect action selection with learning about an articulated object. These examples motivate treating an action as both a task step and an experiment. [cite:ditto] [cite:umpnet] [cite:where2explore]

The challenge is to choose information-seeking actions that are useful under the robot's limits. A small exploratory motion may identify a joint direction, but it also consumes time and can fail if the grasp is poor. Evaluation should compare the benefit of the information with the interaction budget and report errors before and after exploration.

One promising design keeps several plausible joint hypotheses alive during planning, then updates them from motion or contact. The important result is not merely a calibrated uncertainty score; it is whether a robot that uses that uncertainty succeeds and recovers more often than one that commits too early.

sections.heading: Generate environments that change what policies learn
paragraphs: Scene generation offers control over the training distribution. ProcTHOR varies houses, Holodeck translates language into interactive environments, and RoboGen connects generated scenarios to robot learning. Their relevance extends beyond visual diversity: they let researchers ask which variations teach a policy a transferable skill. [cite:procthor] [cite:holodeck] [cite:robogen]

A useful experiment would hold the policy architecture, training budget, and demonstration quantity fixed while changing one aspect of generated scenes: layout, material, articulation, clutter, or task composition. Evaluate on withheld combinations and, when transfer is claimed, on real environments. Otherwise an improvement could be caused by more training rather than a better generation strategy.

Generation should also expose failure cases. A curriculum might deliberately vary handle location, opening clearance, or visual ambiguity after identifying the policy's weak points. The open problem is how to produce challenging but valid tasks without repeatedly exploiting inaccuracies of the simulator or the success detector.

sections.heading: Connect learned world models to physical consequences
paragraphs: A model that predicts plausible future observations can support anticipation, but planning requires those predictions to respond appropriately to alternative actions. Relevant distinctions include whether actions are explicit conditions, whether state persists over long rollouts, and whether a robot can repeatedly act and receive new observations. The embodied-generation and VLA surveys place these questions beside simulation, control, and transfer. [cite:survey-generation-embodied] [cite:survey-vla] The 3D and 4D World Modeling survey further distinguishes image/video, occupancy, and LiDAR representations, emphasizing that the predicted state and evaluation must be specified. [cite:survey-world-modeling]

The cabinet example gives a simple diagnostic. If two candidate actions push in different directions, a predictive model should distinguish their effects on the joint and surrounding objects. A visually convincing sequence that ignores the action can still be useful for generating videos, but it does not supply the intervention model needed by that planner.

A convincing evaluation separates visual quality, geometric consistency, action sensitivity, and decision quality. It should also reward a planner for recognizing when a learned rollout has gone beyond its evidence and for returning to observation or a more constrained model.

sections.heading: Measure the connections, not just the components
paragraphs: Component benchmarks make progress measurable, but a complete claim needs experiments at the interfaces. Improved functional segmentation should be tested for its effect on target selection and manipulation. A more accurate reconstruction should be tested for its effect on collision checking or policy transfer. A larger generated dataset should be tested for the generalization it adds.

These evaluations need controlled substitutions: keep the downstream system fixed, replace one upstream representation, and measure both the intermediate errors and final task outcomes. Include an oracle input to estimate the remaining downstream bottleneck, and a deliberately degraded input to understand sensitivity. This makes a negative result informative: better geometry may not matter if the controller cannot exploit it.
The following table summarizes experiments that would strengthen the links between the survey's areas. They are suggested evaluation designs, not reported results or existing benchmark protocols.

table.caption: Research questions at the boundaries between areas, with suggested evidence that would make progress convincing.
rows: Does a better functional map improve action selection?
Hold the policy fixed; vary predicted, oracle, and degraded part/affordance inputs.
Which geometric and physical errors matter for transfer?
Vary geometry, joints, and dynamics separately; report task sensitivity and real-world outcomes.
Match training compute and data quantity; isolate scene variation; test withheld combinations.
When is exploratory interaction worth its cost?
Track uncertainty, task success, and observation/contact budget before and after exploration.
Are predictions useful under alternative actions?
Compare action-conditioned rollouts and selected actions against measured consequences.

takeaway: The unifying test is simple to state: does a scene representation help an agent choose better, notice an error, or learn from interaction? Progress needs strong components and evidence that the handoffs between them work.
